English.Text: The children want the tale of the young envoy and the desert emir before bed — but I seem to have forgotten half of it. Help me, before they notice!

Every evening, the envoys' children gather for a story, and tonight they have asked for the tale of the young envoy and the desert emir. Unfortunately, the storyteller has forgotten some of its most important turns, and the children are already waiting.
The Envoy needs your help to remember a tale for the children.

Once upon a time, the Sultan sent his youngest envoy, Yunus, into the deep desert. There lived a proud emir whose tribes guarded the only well on the caravan road, and without his friendship, no caravan could pass. When Yunus reached the emir's camp, the guards barred his way. Now, Yunus was... err...
Clever with words, so he told the guards a riddle they could not solve.
Proud and impatient, so he demanded entry in the Sultan's name.

The guards laughed so hard at the riddle that they led Yunus straight to the emir's tent. The old emir sat beside his favourite falcon and regarded him coldly.
"The Sultan wants my well," he said. "Every caravan that drinks from it makes his merchants rich. What will he give me in return?"
So Yunus...
Offered the emir a fair share of the caravan tolls.
Promised the emir a palace of gold he did not have.

The emir stroked his falcon for a long while. "You could have promised me the moon," he said at last, "as the Sultan's envoys usually do. Instead, you offer me what is fair."
The treaty was sealed that very night over bitter coffee. The caravans passed safely for a hundred years, and the emir's grandsons and the Sultan's grandsons called each other brothers.
And that is why, to this day, an envoy's word is worth more than his gold.

The emir's eyes gleamed. "A palace of gold! Very well — my men will guard your caravans until it is built." For a year, the caravans passed in peace. Then the emir travelled to the capital to see his palace... and found nothing but an empty plot of sand.
That is how the War of the Wells began, and it took Yunus the rest of his life to make amends.
And that is why, to this day, an envoy never promises what he cannot give.

The guards cared nothing for the Sultan's name. They took Yunus's dagger and left him alone in a tent for the night. Hungry and humiliated, he lay awake — until, in the middle of the night, the tent flap opened and two shadowy figures crept inside.
Despite his fear, Yunus kept his composure and... hmm...
Drew a hidden knife and threatened them.
Invited them to sit and share his last piece of bread.

"Stay back!" Yunus cried, his knife flashing in the dark. The figures froze — and dropped the plates of food and the pot of coffee they were carrying. They were the emir's own sons, sent to see how the Sultan's envoy would treat strangers in the night.
The next morning, the emir sent Yunus home empty-handed. "A man who greets his guests with a blade," he said, "cannot be trusted with a treaty."
And that is why, to this day, an envoy is judged by how he treats those who cannot help him.

"Please, sit," said Yunus. "I have little, but what I have is yours." The two figures laughed and raised their lamps: they were the emir's sons, carrying a feast — sent by their father to see how the Sultan's envoy would treat strangers in the night.
At dawn, the emir embraced Yunus like a son. "A man who shares his last bread with a stranger," he said, "may drink from my well forever."
And that is why, to this day, the desert tribes say that hospitality opens more doors than any army.
Help the Envoy tell the children a story
